questions.question: In graph-theoretic terms, which statement best captures the idea of connectivity relevant to staged information exchange between two layers of nodes?
questions.choice_A: Every node in the source layer has at least one path to every node in the target layer through directed edges respecting stage order.
questions.choice_B: Every node has at least one undirected edge to some node in the same layer.
questions.choice_C: At least one node in the source layer has a path to at least one node in the target layer.
questions.choice_D: There exists a cycle that visits all nodes in both layers.

questions.question: Which distinction is most useful when reasoning about information flow constraints in computation graphs?
questions.choice_A: A path is any sequence of nodes regardless of edges; a walk requires edges.
questions.choice_B: A path does not repeat vertices, whereas a walk may repeat vertices; this affects whether information can revisit and reuse intermediate states.
questions.choice_C: A trail repeats edges but not vertices; a walk repeats vertices but not edges.
questions.choice_D: A path must be closed, while a walk must be open.

questions.question: Why are layered grid graphs commonly modeled as directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) in staged computation?
questions.choice_A: Because cycles improve throughput but harm latency.
questions.choice_B: Because undirected edges forbid modeling time.
questions.choice_C: Because a DAG enforces a partial order of computation stages, ensuring no information flows backward in time.
questions.choice_D: Because only DAGs can be embedded on grids without crossings.

questions.question: Which property is characteristic of a butterfly network used for routing in staged communication?
questions.choice_A: It minimizes node degree at the expense of path length growing superlogarithmically.
questions.choice_B: It provides unique paths between all source–destination pairs, eliminating congestion.
questions.choice_C: It is an undirected expander optimized for random walks.
questions.choice_D: It has logarithmic depth and structured inter-layer connections that support efficient all-to-all permutations.

questions.question: What distinguishes broadcast trees from multicast trees in communication models?
questions.choice_A: Broadcast trees disseminate from one source to all nodes; multicast trees disseminate from one source to a specified subset of nodes.
questions.choice_B: Broadcast trees require cycles; multicast trees prohibit them.
questions.choice_C: Broadcast trees are always balanced; multicast trees are always unbalanced.
questions.choice_D: Broadcast uses undirected edges; multicast uses directed edges.

questions.question: For complete transmission from layer L to layer L+1 in a directed layered graph, which condition is most directly necessary?
questions.choice_A: Equal number of nodes in L and L+1.
questions.choice_B: For every node u in L and every node v in L+1, there exists a directed path from u to v that does not revisit L.
questions.choice_C: At least one perfect matching between L and L+1 in the undirected sense.
questions.choice_D: Each node in L has out-degree at least two.

questions.question: When counting edges under degree constraints in a layered topology, which statement best captures the degrees-of-freedom perspective?
questions.choice_A: The number of edges equals the number of nodes in any simple graph.
questions.choice_B: Edge count is irrelevant to representational capacity if the graph is acyclic.
questions.choice_C: Given fixed in/out-degree bounds per layer, the total edge budget determines how many independent routing choices (and thus distinct computations) the topology can realize.
questions.choice_D: Degrees of freedom depend only on the number of layers, not on edges.

questions.question: In the unrolled computation graph of matrix multiplication C = AB, what is the graph-theoretic interpretation of intermediate indices (e.g., the summation index k)?
questions.choice_A: They correspond to edge colors enforcing flow conservation.
questions.choice_B: They are terminal sink nodes that absorb flow.
questions.choice_C: They map to cycles ensuring stability of computation.
questions.choice_D: They are internal layer nodes that fan-in from A’s row features and fan-out to B’s column features, mediating multiple paths contributing to each entry of C.

questions.question: How does graph sparsity typically affect information flow and expressivity in staged models?
questions.choice_A: Sparsity can reduce path multiplicity and cut capacities, potentially constraining the diversity of computations and limiting expressivity.
questions.choice_B: Sparsity always improves expressivity by reducing overfitting.
questions.choice_C: Sparsity increases redundancy and therefore robustness.
questions.choice_D: Sparsity forces cycles that increase latency.

questions.question: Which concept most directly links a topology’s ability to sustain throughput with the number of communication steps required for a transfer?
questions.choice_A: Chromatic number
questions.choice_B: Min-cut/max-flow, where the min-cut bounds achievable concurrent transmissions and interacts with depth to determine time-to-deliver.
questions.choice_C: Planarity
questions.choice_D: Graph isomorphism

questions.question: Which statement best distinguishes latency from bandwidth in network design metrics?
questions.choice_A: Latency and bandwidth are identical in DAGs.
questions.choice_B: Latency measures the number of cycles per message; bandwidth measures the number of hops.
questions.choice_C: Latency is dominated by path length (depth) and per-hop delay; bandwidth is dominated by parallel edge capacity enabling multiple messages per unit time.
questions.choice_D: Latency depends only on node degree; bandwidth depends only on clustering coefficient.

questions.question: How does adding redundancy (e.g., extra disjoint paths) affect robustness in communication graphs?
questions.choice_A: It reduces robustness because cycles create deadlocks.
questions.choice_B: It has no effect unless the graph is planar.
questions.choice_C: It only helps if latency is zero.
questions.choice_D: It increases edge/vertex connectivity, improving tolerance to failures and adversarial noise at the cost of additional resources.

questions.question: Why is topological ordering essential for implementing staged information exchange over a DAG?
questions.choice_A: It provides an execution schedule that respects dependencies, ensuring data is produced before it is consumed at each layer.
questions.choice_B: It maximizes the number of cycles in the graph.
questions.choice_C: It minimizes the chromatic number of the graph.
questions.choice_D: It ensures the graph is bipartite.

questions.question: Which network property most directly relates to worst-case point-to-point latency in a connected topology?
questions.choice_A: Clustering coefficient
questions.choice_B: Graph diameter, the maximum shortest-path distance between any pair of nodes
questions.choice_C: Graph density
questions.choice_D: Number of spanning trees

questions.question: From a graph-theoretic viewpoint, what is a plausible consequence of over-parameterizing a communication topology (e.g., adding many extra edges) for a fixed computation?
questions.choice_A: It always reduces path diversity.
questions.choice_B: It forces the graph to become cyclic and unstable.
questions.choice_C: It can increase path multiplicity and cut capacities, potentially enabling higher throughput or robustness but also risking congestion and overfitting-like behaviors without proper scheduling.
questions.choice_D: It makes topological ordering impossible.

questions.question: Why might counting the number of distinct layer-to-layer paths be informative for analyzing a model’s parallelism?
questions.choice_A: Because more paths always decrease redundancy.
questions.choice_B: Because the number of paths equals the number of nodes squared.
questions.choice_C: Because path counts determine the chromatic number of the graph.
questions.choice_D: Because higher path multiplicity often correlates with more independent routes for simultaneous transmissions and richer combinations in composed computations.

questions.question: Compared to tree topologies, which advantage do butterfly networks typically offer for staged communication workloads?
questions.choice_A: Higher bisection bandwidth and support for all-to-all permutations with logarithmic depth, reducing congestion under adversarial traffic compared to naive trees.
questions.choice_B: Zero latency regardless of network size.
questions.choice_C: Unique simple paths that eliminate routing complexity.
questions.choice_D: Lower node degree than a line graph.

questions.question: In a bipartite layered graph between L and L+1 with |L| = m and |L+1| = n, which condition guarantees that any assignment of m inputs can be distinctly delivered to m distinct outputs in L+1 without collisions in a single step?
questions.choice_A: The graph is connected.
questions.choice_B: There exists a matching of size m from L to L+1 (i.e., L is matchable into L+1).
questions.choice_C: Minimum out-degree in L is at least 1.
questions.choice_D: The graph is planar.

questions.question: Which high-level insight underlies communication lower bounds for matrix multiplication in computation graphs?
questions.choice_A: Lower bounds depend only on the number of arithmetic operations, not on data movement.
questions.choice_B: Any layout can arbitrarily reduce data movement below cut capacities by reusing registers indefinitely.
questions.choice_C: Data movement is constrained by locality and cut sizes between data partitions; to supply enough operands, any schedule must move at least a certain amount of data across cuts, implying bandwidth/IO lower bounds.
questions.choice_D: Communication costs vanish if the graph is acyclic.

questions.question: Under what circumstances can a sparse inter-layer topology still support rich information mixing comparable to a denser graph?
questions.choice_A: Only when the graph is a tree.
questions.choice_B: When all nodes have equal degree.
questions.choice_C: When the graph is disconnected into equal components.
questions.choice_D: When the sparse graph is an expander with good spectral gap, providing high connectivity, rapid mixing, and large edge expansion despite low degree.

questions.question: In designing communication networks for staged computations, what is a typical trade-off between latency, bandwidth, and redundancy?
questions.choice_A: Increasing redundancy always decreases both latency and bandwidth.
questions.choice_B: Reducing latency by shortening depth may reduce available parallel edges, lowering bandwidth unless degree or bisection is increased.
questions.choice_C: Maximizing bandwidth always eliminates the need for redundancy.
questions.choice_D: Latency is independent of topology while bandwidth is not.
